Consider a directed weighted graph G(V, E), where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges. Suppose we use adjacency list to implement the graph. Consider a sequence of |V| operations with each corresponding to a different vertex in V. For the operation for vertex v, the cost is assumed to be the number of outgoing edges from v.  (a) What is the cost of the worst possible single operation in this sequence of operations? (b) What is the average amortized cost of the above sequence of operations based on aggregate analysis?

message.content:
The worst possible single operation occurs when a vertex has an edge to every other vertex in the graph, making its cost equal to the maximum number of outgoing edges from any single vertex.

* (a) The worst possible single operation costs **|V| − 1**, since a vertex in a directed graph can have at most one outgoing edge to each of the other |V| − 1 vertices.
* (b) The average amortized cost is **|E| / |V|**, derived from aggregate analysis by dividing the total cost of all |V| operations (which sums to |E|, the total number of edges) by the number of operations.

Wait, let me reconsider. In a directed graph, can we have parallel edges? Typically in standard graph theory, we assume no parallel edges and no self-loops unless specified. So the maximum outgoing edges from any vertex v is |V| - 1.

So the answer to (a) is |V| - 1.

(b) Average amortized cost based on aggregate analysis:
The total cost of the sequence is the sum of the number of outgoing edges from each vertex, which equals |E| (the total number of edges in the graph).

The average amortized cost = Total cost / Number of operations = |E| / |V|.

So the average amortized cost is |E|/|V|.
